source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: A cheatsheet memory that the model rewrites after each query lifts accuracy on math and puzzle streams. But a control arm with the same instructions and an EMPTY memory (DC-) already gets a large part of the gain. So the prompt format, not the stored content, explains part of the effect.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, AIME 2024 (30 questions): baseline 23.3, DC- (empty memory) 36.7, retrieval only 43.3, DC-Cu (cumulative, no retrieval) 50.0, DC-RS (retrieve and synthesise) 46.7. AIME 2025: 6.7, 23.3, 23.3, 36.7, 30.0. GPQA-Diamond (198 q): 59.6, 60.1, 63.6, 61.1, 68.7. GPT-4o AIME 2024: 20.0, 36.7, 26.7, 36.7, 40.0. GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Engineering: baseline 53.2, DC-Cu 44.0 (below baseline), DC-RS 51.2. Full-history append (FH) on AIME 2024: Sonnet 26.7, GPT-4o 6.7 (baseline 20.0).
limits: One run per cell; 30 questions per AIME set, so one question is 3.3 points. Writes happen after EVERY query, not on impasse. No token-matched arm.
agent_relevance: Any memory arm must be compared with an equal-length no-memory arm that carries the same instructions. Otherwise we credit the store for a prompt effect. Appending raw history can be worse than baseline.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: smaller models, Game of 24 and cost remarks
finding: The gain depends on the base model being able to produce correct entries and to use them. Small models gain little or lose. A single discovery (a Python brute-force routine for Game of 24) gives a step change, not a smooth curve, and a model that does not discover it gets nothing.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4o baseline 10, DC- 19, DC-Cu 93, DC-RS 99. Claude 3.5 Sonnet on the same task: 12, 10, 14, 14 (never adopted the code routine). Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2024: 10.0, DC- 26.7, DC-Cu 36.7, DC-RS 30.0; GPQA 43.4, 41.9, 43.7, 49.0. GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024: 16.7, 20.0, 13.3, 13.3 (memory below baseline); GPQA 34.3, 34.3, 33.8, 32.3. Majority vote of 3 on Sonnet: 23.3 on AIME 2024, no gain.
quote: smaller models often fail to retrieve the most relevant past solutions or misapply retrieved knowledge to new problems
limits: Authors say the initial cost of discovering and curating a robust approach 'remains non-trivial' but give no token count. Truncated memory rewrites ('Previous content [...] preserved') were seen.
agent_relevance: Weak models and models that do not find the reusable method gain nothing, so the store gain is gated by generation competence. The Game of 24 jump looks like one compiled rule, not a power-law curve.

source: Cai, Wang, Ma, Chen, Zhou (2024) Large language models as tool makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: A strong model writes a reusable Python tool once from 3 demonstrations and checks it on 3 validation cases. A cheap model then uses the tool. The cheap model reaches the strong model's accuracy and the one-time authoring cost is spread over n uses. This is the clearest cost model in the literature.
numbers: 6 tasks, 240 test instances each. GPT-3.5 CoT vs GPT-3.5 + tool: Logical Deduction 66.4 to 79.7; Tracking Shuffled Objects 61.6 to 99.6; Dyck 20.4 to 92.2; Word Sorting 59.2 to 98.3; Remainder Theorem 0.0 to 100.0; Schedule Meeting 18.9 to 100.0. GPT-4 CoT vs GPT-4 + tool: 88.8 to 86.6 on Logical Deduction (slightly worse), Dyck 63.6 to 87.5. Cost formula: O(nc + C) with tool vs O(nC) for the strong model alone; C more than 15 times c.
limits: Tasks are algorithmic families where one program solves every instance. The cost formula ignores failed tool-making attempts. Only 3 demonstrations; test sets are generated.
agent_relevance: Authoring cost is paid once per task family, so the net saving is positive when a family recurs. Our store has no such guarantee for reasoning items; the saving needs a recurrence rate measured on our stream.

source: Cai et al. (2024) LATM: tool-making success, verification and dispatcher
finding: Tool authoring can fail, and the failure is over-specific tools (work on the 3 training cases only). Execution checks on 3 validation cases rarely repaired anything. A cheap dispatcher that decides 'reuse an existing tool or make a new one' is right about 95 to 96 percent of the time, so about 4 to 5 percent of reuse decisions are wrong.
numbers: Valid tool made (n of 5 trials): GPT-4 maker 3/5 and 4/5 on Logical Deduction and Tracking, 3/5 on Schedule Meeting, 5/5 on the other three; GPT-3.5 maker 0/5 on those three hard tasks (the extracted table's row labels were ambiguous; the text confirms GPT-3.5 failed all 5 trials on the two hard tasks). Tool verification corrected a mistake in only 2 of 60 trials. Dispatcher picks the right existing tool 95% +/- 2%, and decides correctly whether to request tool-making for an unseen task 96% +/- 3%.
quote: the tool is not general enough and may only work on the training samples
limits: Dispatcher test sets are 100 generated instances. It measures family identification, not whether a tool is correct on an out-of-condition input.
agent_relevance: A gate that asks 'does a stored entry apply to this item, or is this a new class' is cheap and about 95 percent right in this setting. It is the nearest thing to a measured precondition check, but it is a classifier on task type, not on conditions.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with LLMs (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: A meta-buffer of high-level thought templates is distilled from solved problems. A new template is stored only when no stored template is similar enough (a miss) or when the distilled template differs from all stored ones. This is a miss-triggered write on reasoning tasks. The paper reports large gains over strong prompting baselines, with about 12 percent of the cost of multi-query methods.
numbers: GPT-4: Game of 24 3.0 standard, 11.0 CoT, 74.0 ToT, 82.4 BoT; Checkmate-in-One 36.4 standard, 49.2 ToT, 86.4 BoT; Geometric Shapes 52.6 to 93.6; MGSM 84.4 to 89.2. Update rule: store only if max cosine similarity to all stored template descriptions is below a threshold (0.5 to 0.7 recommended). Cost about 12% of multi-query methods on average.
limits: Baselines are weak on Game of 24 (3.0). The meta-buffer ablation exists (without it, accuracy falls on Game of 24 and Checkmate) but its figure values could not be matched reliably from the text extraction. Seen only on benchmarks of recurring problem types. The authors admit weaker results on problems needing creativity and with weak-model initialisation. No write-always arm.
agent_relevance: The write-only-on-novelty rule is already in use here but untested against write-always. Template per problem class is a task-class grain, not a subgoal grain.

source: Zhang, Wornow, Wan, Olukotun (2026) Agentic Plan Caching: test-time memory for fast and cost-efficient LLM agents
finding: Plans are cached only after a cache MISS followed by a SUCCESSFUL run. A rule-based filter and a light LLM strip entity names to make a generic template, keyed by an extracted intent keyword. Hits are adapted by a small model. This is the closest published design to 'write only when no stored entry applied, after a verified success'. It cut cost about half at roughly 96.6 percent of full-model accuracy.
numbers: Averages over 5 workloads: cost -50.31%, latency -27.28%, accuracy 96.61% of the accuracy-optimal baseline. FinanceBench (GPT-4o planner, Llama-3.1-8B actor): accuracy-optimal $4.03 at 91.0%; APC $1.86 at 85.5%; hit rate 46%. GAIA: $69.02 at 37.58% to $16.27 at 36.97% (-76.42% cost). QASPER $2.14/58.0% to $0.78/57.0%; AIME 2024 $1.14/64.52% to $0.85/61.29%; AIME 2025 $1.34/61.29% to $0.81/58.06%.
quote: a rule-based filter extracts critical information from the execution log while discarding irrelevant details
limits: No arm that writes after every success, so the effect of the miss-trigger itself is not isolated. Key is an intent keyword, not the accessed facts. Evaluation by a GPT-4o judge. Accuracy loss up to 5.5 points on FinanceBench.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is half answered: a miss-then-verified-success write exists and pays. Still untested: miss-trigger versus write-always at equal tokens, and facts-keyed versus intent-keyed.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Plan Caching: wrong hits, authoring overhead, cache size, cold start
finding: Reusing a stored plan can lower accuracy: with semantic or full-history caching, accuracy on cache hits is clearly below accuracy on misses (a direct measure of wrong application). Keyword matching with exact keys keeps hit accuracy equal to miss accuracy. Loosening the match raises hit rate and cost savings but costs accuracy. Authoring overhead is about 1 percent of cost.
numbers: Cache overhead (keyword extraction plus cache generation) $0.0213 = 1.15% of the FinanceBench total, 1.33% in the worst case with zero hits; TabMWP 0.93% and 1.29%. Fuzzy keyword threshold on FinanceBench: exact 46% hit, $1.86, 85.5% accuracy; above 0.8 similarity 54% hit, $1.15, 83.0%; above 0.6 64% hit, $0.93, 77.0%. Cache size (LRU): 1 entry 2% hit, $3.97, 92%; 10 entries 13%, $3.51, 88%; 20 entries 28%, $2.95, 85%; 50 entries 45%, $1.88, 86%; 100 entries 46%, $1.86, 85.5%. Cold start (100 queries): 15 entries and 14.29% hit at the 20th percentile, 46 entries and 48.00% at the 100th. Derived by me: at about $0.047 saved per hit-rate percentage point and about $0.05 overhead, break-even is near a 1 percent hit rate.
limits: Hit-versus-miss accuracy is shown in a figure (not tabulated). Accuracy falls as the cache grows (92 to 85.5), so more entries is not free. Single dataset for cache size.
agent_relevance: The wrong-application rate is nonzero and rises as matching loosens. Authoring cost is small when the filter is rule-based and a small model writes the template. Net saving is positive at almost any hit rate, but accuracy is the real price.

source: Derived analysis of the Table 7 cold-start numbers in Zhang et al. (2026) APC
finding: Fitting the rate of new cache entries per 20 queries (0.75, 0.60, 0.45, 0.30, 0.20) over the first 100 queries: a straight line fits best, an exponential decay has about 3 times the squared error, and a power law about 29 times. The store is a finite set of intents, so the rate falls to zero at saturation instead of following a smooth power law.
numbers: Grid-search least squares on 5 points (block mid-points 10, 30, 50, 70, 90): linear SSE 0.0010 (0.808 - 0.00694 n); exponential 0.9 exp(-n/66) SSE 0.0032; power 2.18 n^-0.44 SSE 0.0294. Computed by this agent from published table values, one run.
limits: Five points, one run, one dataset, 100 queries. This is NOT a Soar learning-curve fit and cannot separate power from exponential in general.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a power-law stopping rule for the store. Track the new-entry rate directly and stop adding when it nears zero or when the hit-rate gain per entry falls below the authoring cost.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Memp: exploring agent procedural memory
finding: Procedural memory built from the agent's own trajectories (full trajectories plus an abstracted script) raises success and cuts steps on ALFWorld and TravelPlanner for three base models, including Claude 3.5 Sonnet. But on TravelPlanner hard constraints the memory arms are mostly BELOW no memory for GPT-4o and Claude. Even RANDOM retrieval gives most of the commonsense gain.
numbers: ALFWorld test success, no memory to full 'proceduralization': GPT-4o 42.14 to 77.86 (steps 23.76 to 15.01); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 34.97 to 74.72 (24.12 to 15.79); Qwen2.5-72B 41.25 to 77.19 (21.38 to 15.32). Script-only: GPT-4o 56.43, Claude 53.59. TravelPlanner GPT-4o commonsense 71.93 (none), 74.59 (random memories), 73.38 (query key), 76.02 (key = averaged extracted facts); hard-constraint 12.88 (none), 6.72 (random), 8.95 (query), 8.25 (facts), 9.76 (proceduralization). Claude hard constraint 33.06 none vs 29.6 to 30.1 with memory.
limits: Arrow directions were lost in the text extraction; I assume higher is better for both TravelPlanner metrics as in the benchmark. ALFWorld no-memory baselines are low (35 to 42). No equal-token arm.
agent_relevance: Fact-keyed retrieval beat query-keyed by about 2.6 points on GPT-4o commonsense, small. Random memory capturing much of the gain says part of the benefit is a format or prior effect. Memory can trade away constraint satisfaction.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Memp: update strategies, transfer and over-retrieval
finding: Update rules were compared as tasks arrived in groups: append everything (vanilla), keep only successes (validation), and revise a retrieved entry in place when its use failed (adjustment). The error-driven revision was best. Memory from a strong model moved to a weaker one and still helped. Retrieving too many entries lowers performance after a plateau.
numbers: Error-driven update beat the second-best rule by +0.7 reward points and 14 fewer steps by the last task group (figure 3, values from the text). Transfer of GPT-4o's memory to Qwen2.5-14B on TravelPlanner: success +5 percent and 1.6 fewer steps on average; similar on ALFWorld. Memp beat ReAct, ExpeL and AWM on ALFWorld with GPT-4o (figure 4).
quote: retrieving too many memories can lead to a decline in the agent's performance
limits: Figure values for the update rules and transfer were read from text, not tables. The retrieval-count curve was not tabulated. One benchmark per claim.
agent_relevance: Repairing an entry when its reuse fails is the closest published analogue to chunk repair. Admission by success only is not enough; error-driven revision is better. Retrieved count must be capped.

source: Chen et al. (2024) AutoManual: constructing instruction manuals by LLM agents via interactive environmental learning (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Rules are built online while the agent acts and are verified by later episodes. Online building beats offline building from the same trajectories. Raw saved skills cause path dependence: the agent copies past success paths and fails to adapt. Building the manual on ALFWorld cost about 14 US dollars. A task type stops being trained after 3 successes in a row.
numbers: ALFWorld success: AutoManual 97.4 (GPT-4-turbo), 86.2 (GPT-3.5-turbo). Offline rule building: 88.1 to 90.7 (vs 97.4 online). Without skill and reflection libraries 89.5. Without case-conditioned builder prompts 93.8. Rule ablations (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4): no Type attribute 74.6 / 91.5; no Example 76.8 / 92.7; no Validation Logs 85.4 / 97.0; no helper methods 79.6 / 94.3. Building used 6 tasks per task type (36 tasks) and cost about $14 including formulation.
quote: the agent blindly replicates the paths of previous successes, failing to adapt appropriately to new scenarios
limits: Closed ALFWorld with one human demonstration and initial rules. The cost figure is for building only, not for the saving.
agent_relevance: A stop rule ('3 successes in a row means this class is solved') is an inexpensive admission/stop rule used here without an ablation. Typed rules with an example and the conditions of use matter more than the number of rules.

source: Tang et al. (2025) Agent KB: leveraging cross-domain experience for agentic problem solving
finding: Replaying a retrieved workflow is worth less than adapting it to the current case. A disagreement gate (apply a refinement only if its embedding is close to the original plan, cosine at least 0.8) is used against interference. Without the refine step the benefit disappears.
numbers: smolagents + GPT-4.1 on GAIA validation (165 tasks), pass@1 average: baseline 55.15; full Agent KB 61.21; without refine step 55.15; with raw workflow replay 58.18; without retrieve step 57.58; without reason step 60.00. Refine removal costs -6.06 points. The headline gains (55.2 to 73.9) are at pass@3 after failure diagnoses are added.
quote: Removing the Refine stage incurs the largest drop (-6.06), confirming that retrieved workflows must be adapted rather than replayed
limits: Pass@2 and pass@3 use the failures of earlier passes on the same items, so those headline gains are not comparable to one-shot reuse. Only pass@1 is used here.
agent_relevance: Replaying a stored procedure as is loses part of the gain. Adapting before use is a measured improvement (+3.0 points over raw replay, one benchmark), which supports an explicit precondition-and-adapt step.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), ICLR 2026
finding: A playbook of itemised bullets with helpful/harmful counters is updated by small deltas, not full rewrites. Full rewrites cause context collapse, a sudden loss of stored knowledge. Adaptation cost is far below GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet. The store tolerates occasional bad updates but not constant ones. Gains hold, smaller, on a stronger base model.
numbers: Collapse case on AppWorld: at step 60 the context held 18,282 tokens with accuracy 66.7; at the next step it held 122 tokens with accuracy 57.1, below the no-adaptation 63.7. AppWorld, DeepSeek-V3.1: ReAct 42.4 average; plus ICL +3.6; GEPA +4.0; Dynamic Cheatsheet online +9.5; ACE offline +17.0; ACE online +17.1; ACE without ground-truth labels +14.8. GPT-5.1 base 54.2: ACE gains roughly +6 to +11.6, DC +4.7 (table layout garbled). Cost: AppWorld offline GEPA 53,898 s and 1,434 rollouts vs ACE 9,517 s and 357 rollouts (-82.3%, -75.1%); FiNER online DC $17.7 and 65,104 s vs ACE $2.9 and 5,503 s. Harmful-update test on FiNER (base 70.7): a bad update every iteration 66.7 (-4.0); every 5th 76.1; every 10th 77.0; every 25th 77.8; never 78.3.
quote: at the very next step it collapsed to just 122 tokens, with accuracy dropping to 57.1
limits: Table cells read from a garbled extraction, so only figures stated in the text or in clean tables are exact. Harmful updates were injected on purpose, not found naturally. AppWorld and finance only.
agent_relevance: Store maintenance should use small edits with counters, never whole rewrites. A store with a few wrong entries still beats no store; a store that is wrong constantly does not. Counting helpful and harmful uses is a cheap deletion signal not yet tested for false deletions.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory
finding: A streaming benchmark that runs more than ten memory methods over task streams. A plain retrieval baseline (ExpRAG: store each task experience, retrieve similar ones) is competitive. On single-turn reasoning with Claude 3.7 Sonnet most memory modules sit near the no-memory baseline. The gain from memory grows with how similar the tasks in a stream are.
numbers: Single-turn average with Claude 3.7 Sonnet: baseline 0.54; history 0.55; most memory modules between 0.48 and 0.59 (Table 1 layout garbled, per-method cells uncertain). Correlation of ReMem gain with within-dataset task similarity: Pearson r = 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). ReMem step reduction on ALFWorld 22.6 to 11.5. With failed experiences also stored (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, ALFWorld plus ScienceWorld): ReMem average success about 0.81 vs about 0.43 to 0.48 for DC-Cu, DC-RS, AWM, ExpRecent (cells uncertain). Pruning rates: GPQA 36.8%, AIME 17.5% and 10.8%.
limits: Table cells are hard to align in the text extraction; only values that matched on two readings are given. The authors designed ReMem themselves. Pruning is by the agent and there is no test of false deletion.
agent_relevance: On a strong Claude model with reasoning questions, generic memory gives little; gains appear in repeated-structure streams. This is the nearest measurement to gap 8, but it is Claude 3.7 and not our model.

source: Heathcote, Brown, Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 7(2)
finding: Abstract read through Europe PMC; the paper is paywalled and the full text was not opened. Power and exponential functions were fitted to 40 data sets. The exponential fit better in every un-averaged data set, and averaging favoured the power function.
numbers: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments. A new APEX function fit better than a power function with an extra pre-experimental-practice parameter.
quote: The exponential function fitted better than the power function in all the unaveraged data sets.
limits: Full text and fitting method not read. Human tasks, not rule-learning programs.
agent_relevance: Fit per run, not on averages. Averaging across our runs would bias toward a power form, so any Soar-style claim about a power law needs per-run fits. Gap 7 stays open for LLM agents.

source: Evans, Brown, Mewhort, Heathcote (2018) Refining the law of practice, Psychological Review 125(4)
finding: Abstract read through Europe PMC; full text not opened (paywalled). Both power and exponential assume the speed-up always slows. A new law allows an initial delay (slower, faster, slower). It uses hierarchical Bayesian fits that avoid averaging. In a clear majority of paradigms the delayed exponential law was supported.
numbers: No sample sizes in the abstract.
agent_relevance: A learning curve with an initial delay (store empty, then hits start) is expected for a store. The delayed form, not a plain power law, is the form to test on our agent per run.
